title: Sway Sensors for Liability Trees
one_liner: Clamp-on accelerometer nodes that learn each high-consequence tree's own sway signature and alert arborists when it changes, turning one-off tree risk assessments into a recurring monitored service.
customer: Owners of trees with large liability tails: campgrounds and RV parks, historic estates and cemeteries, school districts, HOAs, golf courses and city parks departments. Channel: consulting arborists with tree-risk qualifications, and public-entity insurers and risk pools.
problem: Tree risk assessment is a visual snapshot repeated every few years, yet storms and root decay can change risk overnight. Falling trees kill people in campgrounds and parks and generate large claims. Owners can't watch hundreds of trees, and arborists have no recurring revenue stream.
solution: A MEMS accelerometer and inclinometer node on the trunk (BOM in the tens of dollars) reporting sway frequency, damping and static tilt over LoRaWAN. Each tree is modeled against its own baseline plus local wind data. Anomalies such as a drop in natural frequency or new tilt trigger an arborist inspection within 24 hours. Annual reports combine the data with the arborist's assessment as a documented notice-and-response record. Deploy on the top 5-10% of trees over targets: tent pads, cabins, playgrounds.
why_now: Published work now supports the approach: LoRaWAN tree-tilt systems recorded failure modes during a super typhoon, and 2025-26 papers validate low-cost MEMS inclinometers and accelerometers for tree stability analysis. Cheap LoRaWAN gateways and stronger storm and drought volatility raise demand.
revenue_model: USD 8-15 per sensor per month plus a USD 99 hardware deposit. Arborist resellers keep about 30% and bill their own assessments. A 40-tree campground is about USD 6k per year. Insurer-funded programs for risk pools later.
non_obvious_insight: Don't try to predict failure. Trees differ, so each tree's own baseline is the model and change is the signal. The buyer's real purchase is documented reasonable care: proof of what they knew and when they acted. That also flips arborists from selling a triennial visual inspection to owning a recurring alert service.
first_30_days: Put off-the-shelf LoRa accelerometer nodes on 20 trees with two consulting arborists and one friendly campground or state park. Collect 90 days of sway data across a wind season. Partner with a university forestry program for validation and a publishable result. Sell the first pilot subscriptions to campgrounds at about USD 600 per year per site.

title: Farm Income Dial: ACA Cliff Management
one_liner: A December planning service that uses the grain-contract and input-prepay levers farmers already control to keep household income under the 400% poverty cliff and avoid repaying a full year of health subsidies.
customer: Farm families who buy ACA marketplace coverage. KFF estimates about 27% of farmers do, nearly triple the adult average. The co-op grain desks and rural CPA firms that advise them pay for a white-label version.
problem: The enhanced ACA subsidies expired on December 31, 2025, so the hard cutoff at 400% of poverty is back (roughly $130k for a family of four). The 2025 tax law also removed repayment caps for tax year 2026. A farm family that projected income under the line and then lands $2,000 over must repay every dollar of advance credits, often $15k to $25k. Farm income is lumpy and depends on prices and yields nobody knows in January. Farm CPAs optimize the federal tax bracket, not the ACA cliff, and nobody connects the two.
solution: Farmers connect their grain settlements, deferred contracts, prepaid inputs and equipment purchases. The tool tracks estimated 2026 MAGI against the cliff and gives a concrete action list: how many bushels to defer into 2027, how much fertilizer to prepay, when to elect CCC loan treatment, when to buy equipment. It also models plan choice for 2027 open enrollment, including Farm Bureau non-ACA plans and their underwriting risks. Every recommendation is reviewed by the household's CPA, so this is planning software and not tax advice.
why_now: This is the first tax year with no repayment cap and no enhanced credits. Marketplace enrollment fell from 22.1M to 19.2M in a year. The planning window closes December 31, 2026, and every Iowa farm family on a marketplace plan is exposed right now.
revenue_model: $350 to $600 per farm household per season. Broker commissions from carriers when the tool places 2027 coverage. White-label licenses to rural CPA firms and co-op grain desks ($50 to $100 per client). Optional success fee of 10% of the protected credit.
non_obvious_insight: The ACA cliff is controlled with the same pen that signs deferred-payment contracts. The co-op grain desk is the real MAGI control panel for farm families. CPAs do not see it because they only meet clients in February, after the levers are gone.
first_30_days: Partner with 2 rural CPA firms and one co-op grain desk. Build a spreadsheet-grade calculator plus a one-page 'cliff letter' for clients. Run a 'Cliff Night' at the co-op with farm families in October and November. Convert 30 to 50 households at $350 before the December deadline and document dollars saved.

title: Right-Size Rx: Deprescribing After GLP-1 Starts
one_liner: Pharmacist outreach that adjusts insulin, sulfonylureas and BP meds in the weeks after a GLP-1 start, sold to payers on avoided harm and drug spend.
customer: Medicare Advantage plans, Medicaid MCOs, ACOs and self-funded employers with large diabetic and hypertensive populations.
problem: Tirzepatide trial protocols recommend cutting sulfonylureas by at least 50% and basal insulin by at least 20% at start, because GLP-1 weight loss lowers glucose and blood pressure. In real practice nobody is triggered or paid to do this, so patients face hypoglycemia, hypotension and falls, while brand diabetes drugs (SGLT2s, DPP-4s) keep getting refilled.
solution: Claims-triggered (and pharmacy-partner-triggered for cash-pay fills) pharmacist outreach at days 7-28 after first fill among patients on insulin, SU or antihypertensives. Collaborative-practice protocols to adjust or recommend changes, home BP and CGM review, and a savings and safety ledger for the payer.
why_now: The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge started Jul 1, 2026 and cash pills at $149-$299 are pushing GLP-1s into older, more medicated patients. Payers are fixated on the GLP-1 price line and are missing the neighboring drug lines.
revenue_model: $2-4 per targeted member per month, or $250 per completed episode, plus a share of measurable avoided ED visits and drug savings.
non_obvious_insight: The near-term safety and cost of GLP-1s sits in the other drugs on the patient's list. Payers can offset part of the GLP-1 cost by trimming those, so it belongs on a CFO's line item, not just a quality dashboard.
first_30_days: Approach one regional MA plan or IPA and one pharmacist group. Run a 90-day pilot on 300 patients identified from Rx claims. Measure interventions made, hypoglycemia events and avoided fills, and hand back a savings ledger.

title: Worker-Owned Agentic Back-Office Cooperatives
one_liner: A franchise-in-a-box that helps laid-off finance and admin staff form co-ops running agent-leveraged bookkeeping, payroll and billing services for local small businesses, keeping the surplus themselves.
customer: Small businesses (5-50 employees) pay $600-2,500 a month. The co-ops pay a 5-8% platform fee, and are financed by cooperative-lending CDFIs, SBA microloans and workforce boards.
problem: The AI productivity dividend flows to platform owners while back-office workers lose jobs. Small businesses lack trusted human accountability (Bench's Dec 2024 shutdown stranded about 35k SMBs), and pure-AI bookkeepers still need a human on the hook.
solution: Co-op charter templates under state worker-co-op law, a shared agent stack (ledger automation, document intake, reconciliation) so each member handles 30-60 clients, a shared E&O policy, bank account and brand, client acquisition through local CPAs and chambers, and patronage dividends. Six-week onboarding.
why_now: Agentic accounting can now handle high-volume categorisation and reconciliation, finance-ops layoffs are rising, Bench's collapse left an opening, and co-op-friendly state laws and CDFI capital exist.
revenue_model: 5-8% of co-op revenue as a platform fee, tooling margin and $5-10k implementation fees per co-op.
non_obvious_insight: Ownership is the lever: workers who own the margin adopt agents fully, whereas employees hide productivity gains for fear of layoff. The scarce asset is trusted local human accountability, and agents supply the cost side.
first_30_days: Find 8-10 laid-off bookkeepers and controllers in one metro through layoff communities. Form a pilot co-op with a co-op legal clinic. Sign 15 SMB clients via three local CPAs and a chamber and run the first monthly closes.

title: Fake-Support Scam Takedown for Fintechs
one_liner: A monitoring and takedown service that finds scammers posing as your customer support in public help threads, clusters them by phone, WhatsApp and Telegram identifiers, and kills them fast with regulator-ready evidence files.
customer: Fraud, trust & safety and CX heads at crypto exchanges, wallet makers, neobanks, BNPL and payment providers. Start with mid-market crypto/fintech ($5M-$50M ARR), then EU payment service providers. Roughly $3k-$10k per month.
problem: Every 'my account is locked' thread in a fintech or crypto subreddit gets a friendly stranger reply within minutes, then a DM pushing a WhatsApp or Telegram 'support agent'. Mods remove the comments, but the brand never sees removed comments or DMs. The same 20-50 phone numbers and handles recycle week after week, and victims are usually novices or seniors. Mods keep private spreadsheets of these identifiers, and nobody aggregates them for the brand being impersonated.
solution: Monitor public help venues (Reddit through licensed access or partners, plus X, Facebook groups, YouTube comments, Google Business listings, review-site replies and search ads) for support-impersonation patterns. Extract the contact identifiers, graph-cluster them into campaigns, and file takedowns with WhatsApp/Telegram, telcos, registrars and platforms. Produce timestamped evidence packs for refund disputes and regulators. Give each brand a pre-registered 'official support channels' beacon that community mods can add to a sticky or AutoMod reply for free, cutting victim conversion without any content moderation. Mods are never paid, and the data flows to them.
why_now: The EU PSR/PSD3 political agreement of 27 November 2025 makes payment providers refund customers in bank-employee impersonation scams and makes online platforms liable to those providers if they fail to remove notified fraudulent content. Notification evidence and takedown speed now have a dollar value. The UK's mandatory APP-fraud reimbursement (since October 2024) already priced this risk. LLM-written scam scripts are fluent, which defeats keyword filters.
revenue_model: SaaS subscription of $3k-$10k per month per brand, a per-takedown premium tier, evidence-pack retainers for payment providers in the EU, and later an identifier feed sold to telcos and platforms.
non_obvious_insight: The scam's weak point is the contact channel, not the message. Fluent AI text is cheap, but the phone numbers, handles and domains are a small recyclable set, so identifier graphs beat content classifiers. Mod removal logs also hold the ground truth on how many minutes a scam reply survives, which brands can't see and which now matters for liability. An 'official channels' sticky is the cheapest conversion-killer there is.
first_30_days: Build a free 'exposure audit' for 10 mid-size crypto and fintech brands: a 30-day scan of public threads, X and Google Business listings that shows them 40 live scam identifiers and how long each survived. Send each fraud lead their own brand's data. Convert 2 into $2.5k/month paid pilots. Partner with 3 volunteer mod teams of fintech subreddits, giving them free tooling and taking labeled ground truth in return, with no payment to mods.

title: Factory-Slot Exchange for Transformers and Switchgear
one_liner: A verified marketplace and escrow for reassigning manufacturer production slots, the truly scarce asset, from stranded projects to shovel-ready buyers.
customer: Municipal utilities and rural electric co-ops that hyperscaler orders are crowding out, independent power producers, EPC procurement leads, and developers whose projects are stalled by moratoria or interconnection withdrawals and who hold deposit-backed slots they cannot use.
problem: Substation transformer lead times have stretched from about 140 weeks in 2023 to more than 160 weeks in 2026, and medium-voltage gear is at two to three years. Industry estimates say 30-50% of planned 2026 US data center capacity could slip on equipment alone. Slots are reserved years ahead with deposits, and when a project dies (a moratorium, a lost interconnection position) the slot is orphaned. Slot trading happens by handshake in whisper networks, with no verification and no title.
solution: A slot registry plus escrowed transfer. (1) Verify each slot with the manufacturer: spec, kVA and voltage class, delivery window, deposit status. (2) Get manufacturer consent, which is easier if you give them cleaner backlog data. (3) Match buyers using a small technical team of retired utility engineers who know which specs can be re-specified. (4) Hold funds in escrow and transfer title. Publish an index of slot pricing by spec, which is the first public price signal for the shortage.
why_now: Lead times are at record highs in 2026, and new state permit pauses (New York, Texas) are orphaning slots that speculative developers reserved. Small utilities lost their traditional access to equipment as hyperscalers bought capacity, which creates political goodwill for a neutral exchange.
revenue_model: A 2-4% fee on the purchase order value from the buyer and about 1% from the seller. Paid verification dossiers for sellers, and a subscription for the slot price index and alerts.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is the production slot with a spec, not the physical box. Because many slots can be re-specified within tolerance, a technical matchmaker unlocks supply that looks fungible only to insiders. The people hurt most, small utilities, are also the best-motivated and least-served buyers, so serving them is both profitable and defensible.
first_30_days: Recruit two retired utility procurement engineers as advisors. Cold-outreach 50 EPC procurement leads and 20 co-ops (start at NRECA-type meetings and LinkedIn). Collect five slot listings from stalled projects. Broker one transfer manually with a lawyer-drafted escrow agreement and no software. Charge the fee on that deal and use it as proof for the manufacturers.

title: Hard-Stop Fuse and Warranty for AI Cloud Bills
one_liner: A free scanner finds unrestricted legacy Google/Firebase and Bedrock exposure, installs a real hard kill-switch, and later sells a capped bill-shock warranty only to accounts that have the fuse installed.
customer: Seed-stage startups, solo developers and small agencies running LLM calls on GCP/Firebase or AWS Bedrock, including anyone running coding agents unattended. They pay $29-49/month per cloud account for the fuse and monitoring, and a small warranty premium later.
problem: Cloud providers ship alerts and credits, not hard caps, and they often refuse refunds. A Bedrock user ran up $37,901.73 through a LiteLLM + prompt-caching miss and asked 'why can I not say this IAM principal may spend at most $200/month'. A 2016 Firebase Android key generated $67k of Gemini charges in 19 hours, and Google support said it was 'unable to make adjustments'. A Claude Code user burned $2,000+ without noticing. A founder's $4,200 fraudulent Gemini charge was followed by suspension of a $1M ARR company's whole Google Cloud project.
solution: Step 1, a read-only CLI/web scanner that lists unrestricted API keys, projects with Gemini or Bedrock enabled, forgotten legacy Firebase keys (which the May 2024 auto-restriction policy missed in at least one documented case), and missing budget actions. Step 2, a one-click installer for hard stops: key restrictions and quota overrides on GCP, and on AWS Budget Actions that attach an IAM/SCP deny on model invocation. Step 3, per-minute anomaly detection that trips the fuse in seconds, not at the next daily billing rollup. Step 4, once an account has run fused for 30+ days, a capped bill-shock warranty (start at $5k, backed by a small reserve, later an MGA or reinsurer) priced from the loss data the fuse collects.
why_now: Unattended agents with huge contexts and Opus-class pricing turned ordinary integration mistakes into five-figure invoices in 2026. Gemini access now hangs off keys created years before Gemini existed. Google and AWS are visibly not shipping hard caps: the April 2026 $67k Gemini case was denied adjustment as of May 2026, and the $37.9k Bedrock case is from April 2026.
revenue_model: Free scan (lead gen). $29/month per cloud account for fuse plus monitoring, $49 for multi-project agencies. $199 one-off audit-and-install for agencies. Warranty add-on priced at roughly 2-4% of the covered limit per year, sold only to fused accounts.
non_obvious_insight: The clouds have shown the market will not get hard caps or reliable refunds from them, so the insurable unit is a fused account, not a customer. The technical control doubles as underwriting, and every victim thread is a warm lead. Evidence: $37,901.73 Bedrock bill with the 'hard spend limit' complaint https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47933355; $67k in 19 hours with Google denying adjustment and other victims reporting $13,000 and £2,700 https://discuss.ai.google.dev/t/unexpected-67k-gemini-api-spike-in-19-hours-2016-firebase-provisioned-android-key-not-covered-by-googles-may-2024-auto-restriction-policy/142717; $1M ARR startup suspended after a compromised key https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48396596; $2,000+ Claude Code invoice https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46851021. Caveat: refunds are not reliably obtainable, so do not lead with a claims-desk model.
first_30_days: Week 1-2: build the GCP key/Gemini exposure scanner on top of Cloud Asset Inventory and publish 'Check your 2016 Firebase keys' on HN and the Google AI forum thread. Week 3: add an AWS CloudFormation one-click Budget Action deny for Bedrock. Week 4: DM the authors and repliers of the public bill-shock threads, plus agencies, and offer a $199 audit-and-install to the first 20; convert them to $29/month monitoring. Log every trip event and near-miss to build the actuarial base for the warranty.

title: Flood Cover Sold to the Lender
one_liner: Homeowners won't buy flood insurance, but the bank holding their mortgage should, because the uninsured flood loss lands on the lender's collateral.
customer: Community banks, credit unions and non-bank mortgage servicers with concentrated mortgage exposure outside FEMA high-risk zones, where flood cover isn't mandatory.
problem: Moody's puts uninsured US flood exposure at $375B-$1T. Private flood capacity is growing but 'customers aren't buying' (Insurance Business, 2026-07-22). Outside mandatory-purchase zones, borrowers skip cover, then walk or go delinquent after a flood and leave the lender with damaged collateral.
solution: Two steps. First, a parcel-level flood-exposure audit of the lender's book. Second, a lender-paid group or blanket flood policy (indemnity with a parametric fast-pay component) for the highest-risk non-mandatory loans, with disclosure and an opt-out. It is delivered as an MGA program on existing private flood capacity, and regulatory structure is validated state by state.
why_now: Private flood capacity is expanding (Neptune passed 300k policies and $400M premium). Reinsurance is softening, so capacity is cheap. Record cat bond issuance ($65.6B outstanding) shows abundant capital, and bank regulators are asking about climate concentration.
revenue_model: MGA commission and policy fees (roughly 10-20% of premium) plus a $15k-$40k paid portfolio audit per lender.
non_obvious_insight: The demand problem is really a distribution problem. Selling to 10,000 skeptical homeowners is expensive, while selling to one lender covers thousands of borrowers. The party with the incentive to buy is the one who bears the unmandated loss.
first_30_days: Run free flood-exposure audits for 20 credit unions in river and Gulf states using public mortgage data and open flood models. Line up a licensed surplus-lines partner. Sell one paid pilot covering about 500 highest-risk loans.

title: Contingency Audit of Unbilled Plumbing Materials
one_liner: Reconcile a trade shop's supply-house invoices against its customer invoices and catch both parts that were bought but never billed and quiet supplier price drift, paid a percentage of what gets recovered.
customer: Plumbing, HVAC and electrical shops doing $1.5-15M in revenue with 5-40 techs, running ServiceTitan, Housecall Pro or Jobber plus QuickBooks, buying on account from Ferguson, Hajoca, Winsupply or a local supply house.
problem: Shops lose margin in two places nobody watches. First, parts go out on a supply-house ticket with a job name, or come off the truck stock, and never make it onto the customer invoice. Techs charge the labor from the flat-rate book and forget the $6 valve, the wax ring, the supply lines, the $40 of fittings. In the shops I know, when the office finally reconciles a quarter it is typically a few percent of revenue. Second, supply houses price off list with a contractor multiplier, and list prices have moved several times since the Section 232 copper, steel and aluminum tariffs (50%, working through a long manufacturer-to-contractor lag). Surcharges appear, job-quoted prices are not honored, returns credits are never issued, and no owner has time to read 40 invoices a week.
solution: Shops set up an email forwarding rule for supply-house invoices and statements and give us read access to their field-service software export. An LLM-based line-item parser ties supply-house lines to jobs and POs, then produces a weekly leak list for the office manager: (1) purchased-not-billed by job, (2) price versus the shop's own multiplier and versus the same SKU 30 days ago, (3) unclaimed return credits, (4) pricebook items where cost has risen past the target markup, with a repricing file ready to import. Later add a benchmark ('you pay 9% more than shops your size for PEX-A fittings') built from pooled anonymized invoices, which is the moat.
why_now: Tariff-driven price volatility means flat-rate pricebooks are stale within a quarter, and owners know it. Invoice parsing with LLMs went from a custom-ML project to an afternoon. Field-service platforms expose APIs and exports. The trades are also ahead of everyone else in adopting software but behind in auditing it, so there is no incumbent audit product.
revenue_model: Contingency fee of 25% of recovered and newly captured revenue for the first 12 months (no recovery, no fee), converting to a $199-499 per month subscription for continuous monitoring plus the pricing benchmark. Data licensing of the pooled price index to distributors and manufacturers later.
non_obvious_insight: Owners obsess over lead cost and tech hiring while the highest-ROI dollar is sitting in the shoebox of paid invoices. Everything a tech installs was bought on a ticket with a job name on it, so the truth is already in two systems that have never been compared. This is the freight-audit and telecom-audit model, and no one has brought it to the trades because the people who feel the pain are too busy running trucks to build it.
first_30_days: Offer a free 90-day audit to 10 shop owners from a peer group (a PHCC chapter, Nexstar or Service Roundtable style mastermind). Have them forward statements and give a one-time export. Turn each audit around in 48 hours with a single 'found money' number and a list of specific invoices. Convert the shops with the largest number to the contingency contract. A spreadsheet plus an LLM parsing script is enough for the first ten.

title: Driver-Sourced Dock Queue Index for Funds
one_liner: Pay verified truckers to report what they see at plants, ports and distribution centers, and sell the resulting real-economy index to funds, credit analysts and site-selection teams.
customer: Small and mid-size quant and fundamental hedge funds, equity and credit research shops covering industrials and retail, private-credit lenders to retailers and manufacturers, and commercial real-estate investors. Annual subscriptions of $25k to $150k per sector index.
problem: Alt-data vendors see parking lots from satellites and card swipes from panels, but nobody sees the freight dock. Telematics vendors sell dwell time at a geofence but not what's moving, whether the yard is full, or whether appointments are being cancelled. Tariff shocks in 2025 to 2026 made import front-loading, steel inventory builds and retailer DC slowdowns critical to read weeks earlier. The alt-data market was about $2.8B in 2025 and most institutional funds use several sources, but trucking signals stay coarse.
solution: A watchlist of about 500 facilities mapped to public tickers (steel mills, Amazon and Walmart DCs, Home Depot and Costco DCs, auto plants, ports and rail ramps). Drivers whose ELD or phone geofence confirms they are at the site file a 30-second structured report: queue length, hours waited, outbound commodity, trailers stacked or pulled, yard fullness, appointments cancelled, 'no freight today'. Pay $3 to $8 per accepted report. Aggregate into weekly facility, sector and regional indices. Only publicly observable facts are collected, with no shipper confidential documents and no insider employees. A securities lawyer reviews the collection rules before launch.
why_now: Tariff-driven import and inventory swings make physical-economy signals more valuable than ever. Freight recession conditions mean lots of idle drivers willing to earn side income while waiting. Geofence verification, instant payouts and modern OCR/LLM structuring make a human-observation network cheap to run. Fund appetite for differentiated alt data is high because standard satellite and card data are commoditized.
revenue_model: Sector-index subscriptions of $30k to $150k a year, custom facility watchlists, a raw API tier, and per-project reports for private-credit lenders and site-selection teams. Drivers are paid per report, so unit economics are strongly positive.
non_obvious_insight: Truckers are the only people who physically stand in line at the real economy every day. A driver notices 'the mill's outbound lot is empty at 2pm Tuesday' or 'this DC is turning away appointments' weeks before it shows up in ISM or earnings. Telematics sells dwell minutes, but only a human sees the commodity mix, the closed dock doors and the mood in the queue, and drivers already trade this information on CB and in Facebook groups for free. This is a new data category, not an improvement to freight software.
first_30_days: Recruit 100 drivers across three freight regions (Gulf Coast, Midwest steel belt, Inland Empire) via Facebook groups and pay $5 per accepted report via instant payment. Cover 20 facilities weekly for 4 weeks. Backtest the index against public earnings and shipment data. Pitch 10 small funds through alt-data brokers and direct outreach with a free 30-day trial on 10 tickers. Charge $2k to $5k a month pilots after the trial.

title: Agent-Access Terms Index for Enterprises
one_liner: A living database and alert feed of what the top 500 SaaS and data vendors allow, meter and prohibit when your AI agents touch their APIs and data.
customer: General counsel, procurement and IT platform leads at 100-5,000 employee companies deploying agents, plus their outside counsel. SaaS vendors are a later customer.
problem: Most insiders read the Ninth Circuit ruling (the user, not the agent vendor, accessed Amazon) as 'agents can roam free'. For enterprises it means the fight moves to contract, and the user's company is the bound party. Vendors are already moving. SAP restricts third-party AI agent access to its APIs, Slack has throttled non-Marketplace apps and banned persistent indexes, and ServiceNow throttles inbound agent traffic. Vendors are also adding agent-action meters. No one tracks any of this, so a company can breach terms at a dozen vendors and learn about it from a suspension or audit letter.
solution: Build a structured agent-use rights matrix for about 500 vendors: allowed, banned or priced, rate limits, indexing, retention and training clauses, and official connector alternatives. Add change detection on terms and API policy pages with plain-English diffs. Add a connector that maps your OAuth-connected apps and agent inventory to the matrix and flags conflicts. Include a clause library, negotiation playbooks and an audit-defense pack.
why_now: Platform lockdowns (SAP, Slack, ServiceNow) and per-agent-action pricing arrived in 2025-26, and the Ninth Circuit ruling (August 2026) made contract the main battleground. Amazon can still seek rehearing, which adds uncertainty buyers want tracked.
revenue_model: $1.5-5k/month subscriptions for legal and procurement teams, $8-25k fixed-fee exposure reviews and negotiation packages, and later vendor-side benchmarking.
non_obvious_insight: Contract terms are becoming the price list and permission system of the agent economy, and they sit in unstructured legalese nobody indexes. The index is also the negotiating leverage, because it shows a buyer what comparable vendors concede.
first_30_days: Have an LLM plus a contract lawyer parse the terms and API policies of the top 100 SaaS vendors. Publish a free Agent Rights Scorecard for 25 of them to generate inbound. Sign 5 design partners at $1.5k/month and offer a $8-15k agent contract exposure review.

title: Error-Rate Cliff Insurance for SNAP Agencies
one_liner: A managed QC service that re-reads a sample of newly approved and recertified SNAP cases against federal review rules and builds federal-dispute packets, sold to county and state agencies facing cost-share penalties.
customer: County social-services directors in county-administered states (NC, CO, MN, NY, OH, VA and others), state QC units, and state agencies with error rates at or above 6%. In FY2025, 20 states were at 10% or higher.
problem: Illinois's FY2025 SNAP error rate was 14.7%. Its DHS estimates roughly $700M of penalty exposure, is hiring 450 staff for $55M, and faces admin costs rising from $60M to $100M as the state share of SNAP admin costs goes from 50% to 75% in October 2026. In North Carolina, Wilson County's DSS (about $13M budget) faces up to $4.2M in penalties with no state relief, and the state's eligibility system (NC FAST) has no document portal or AI. Counties report ~10% vacancy and staff with about a year of experience. Illinois DHS says most errors are 'minor errors', and the federal definition of an error is any variance of $57 or more.
solution: Each week, supervisors upload a 5-10% sample of case files per caseworker. AI extracts income, household composition, deductions and verification documents, recomputes the benefit under federal and state policy, and flags variances of $57 or more with the policy citation. Supervisors get a fix-before-QC list. For cases in the federal QC sample, the tool builds the dispute or arbitration packet comparing the state review with the federal findings. Certified ex-state QC reviewers sign off on anything high-stakes. Deploy inside the county's own cloud tenant so no PII leaves.
why_now: H.R. 1 shifts benefit-cost sharing to states by error-rate tier, with the top tier at 15% of benefit costs for rates of 10% or more. Penalties begin in FY2028-29, starting October 2027 per Capitol News Illinois. The admin-cost shift hits October 2026. Agencies are also absorbing Medicaid work-requirement workloads, so they cannot hire their way to accuracy.
revenue_model: Per-case-reviewed fee ($15-40 range to test) or annual county subscription of $40-150k. For comparison, one county eligibility worker costs $40-95k a year. Optional shared-savings pricing tied to avoided penalty tier.
non_obvious_insight: The penalty is a cliff function by error-rate band, so fixing a handful of cases near a threshold can be worth millions, which makes a cheap second-look service priced like insurance. In county-administered states, each of ~100 counties (NC) is a separate small buyer that carries its own penalty exposure. The cost of the problem is in the evidence: Illinois's 14.7% rate, ~$700M exposure, 450 hires and $55M budget (https://capitolnewsillinois.com/news/illinois-food-assistance-error-rate-continues-to-grow-as-federal-penalties-loom/). NC's 10% vacancy, Wilson County's $4.2M penalty exposure on a $13M budget, and staff with 11-13 months' experience (https://www.northcarolinahealthnews.org/2026/04/30/medicaid-work-county-challenges/). Job-posting signal: governmentjobs.com showed about 2,000 'eligibility worker' results on 2026-09-28 at roughly $40-95k salaries (https://www.governmentjobs.com/jobs?keyword=eligibility%20worker). Indiana is hiring 400 people to check eligibility (https://indianacapitalchronicle.com/2026/04/29/fssa-hiring-400-medicaid-eligibility-checkers-ahead-of-work-requirements/) and Pennsylvania has about 400 open county positions (https://kffhealthnews.org/medicaid/medicaid-cuts-work-requirements-state-staff-shortages/). Caveat: the tier percentages and FY start dates come from the article and my recollection of the law and should be re-verified.
first_30_days: Target North Carolina, where about 100 counties buy independently in small increments. Recruit 2 retired state QC reviewers as advisers. Offer 3 county DSS directors a free retrospective audit of 100 closed cases, showing errors the county's own review missed. Convert to a paid pilot under the county's small-purchase threshold. Confirm security requirements (in-tenant deployment, redaction) before touching real case files.

title: Exoskeleton Hike Rentals for Active Older Adults
one_liner: Trailhead rental hubs and guided exo-hikes that let 60-80 year-olds keep climbing with powered hip assist.
customer: Active adults 55+ (pay $70-120 per day), outdoor retailers and outfitters, senior-living activity directors and trail-gateway towns.
problem: Consumer exoskeletons now exist ($900-2,300, with the leader's models at about $2,000-2,300) but buyers hesitate to spend that on something they have never tried, and older hikers quietly stop hiking as knees and hips fade.
solution: A rental fleet with fitting, safety briefing and waivers, guided group hikes, retailer rental corners, and monthly exo-walks for senior living communities. Renters get a credit toward purchase and we earn affiliate commissions.
why_now: Consumer hip-assist exoskeletons reached the $900-2,300 range with heavy marketing, the leading brand is pushing an 'offline' era with retail and rental hubs, and the active-older-adult demographic is driving the category.
revenue_model: $79 per day rentals, $30 per person guided add-ons, 8-12 percent affiliate on purchases, retail rental-program fees and $1-2k per month senior-living contracts.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is trial, not price, and manufacturers lack local operators; a small team can own the try-before-you-buy channel. The real work is waivers, fitting and injury protocols, which are also the moat.
first_30_days: Buy or borrow four units (about $8k), set up demo weekends at one or two outdoor shops or campgrounds near a popular trail, run a senior-center exo-walk, and start charging rentals from week two.

title: Universal Viva: AI-Run Oral Verification
one_liner: After each major submission the student takes a five-minute identity-verified voice conversation with an AI examiner about their own work, and humans review only the flagged mismatches.
customer: Online and community-college programs, university departments, dual-enrollment providers and credentialing bootcamps (department chairs and deans), later honor councils.
problem: At Harvard 89% of professors received suspected AI work but only 12% referred cases, and 67% say AI hurts their courses. Detectors are unreliable and biased against non-native writers (lower-confidence data). Oral exams work but do not scale: 300 students at 15 minutes each is 75 hours.
solution: A voice agent reads the submission, asks 6-8 adaptive questions on reasoning, sources and choices, checks consistency with the submitted work, and returns a comprehension score. Low-scoring cases go to a bench of trained human examiners. It measures whether the student understands the work rather than accusing anyone of using AI, with accommodations for disabilities and language.
why_now: Real-time voice models with natural turn-taking and low latency matured in 2025-26. Faculty sentiment has turned sharply negative and detection has failed, so institutions need a fairer alternative before the next term's grades.
revenue_model: $3-6 per verification paid by the institution or $30 per student per course, with premium pricing for human audit and site licenses.
non_obvious_insight: Detection asks 'did an AI write this?', which is unanswerable and adversarial. Verification asks 'does the student understand this?', which is answerable, fairer to non-native writers, and much harder to outsource live in a voice conversation.
first_30_days: Pilot with 3 professors in writing-intensive intro courses at a community college, about 60 students. Compare oral-comprehension scores with graded essays and show an instructor dashboard. Move to $4 per verification after the pilot. Set voice-data retention and accessibility policies before launch.

title: Lot Vault: Reagent Warranty Claims and Lot Registry
one_liner: A photo-the-label app that files unclaimed reagent-guarantee refunds for labs, quietly builds the only lot-level reagent performance database, and then group-buys locked good lots for small labs.
customer: Lab managers and PIs in organoid, iPSC, primary-immune-cell and antibody-heavy labs (about $79-199/month per lab). Core facilities and departments with central purchasing pay for the site-wide tier. Later, challenger reagent vendors and distributors pay for lot-level analytics.
problem: Every experienced postdoc knows the hidden variable behind failed experiments is the reagent lot: FBS, Matrigel/BME, B27, human serum, antibodies, polymerases. A lot that passes the vendor's certificate of analysis can still kill your organoids, and nobody logs lot numbers. Vendors' satisfaction guarantees require the lot number, images and a claim inside a time window, so postdocs almost never file. Money goes unclaimed. Six labs across town hit the same bad lot and never find out. When a good lot runs out, a two-year experimental series has to be re-validated.
solution: Wedge: a phone app where the postdoc snaps the vial label and taps 'worked' or 'failed', with optional gel or blot photos. On 'failed' it drafts the vendor guarantee claim with lot, dates and images, and tracks the credit. On 'worked' it logs the lot against the user's cell type and assay. Over time this becomes a crowd-sourced registry: 'Matrigel lot X: 7 of 9 organoid labs report failure.' Phase 2: when a lot shows good in at least 5 labs, the company negotiates a vendor lot reservation and runs a pooled group buy. Small labs get a locked lot for 12-24 months without needing 100 bottles of freezer space. The company takes a 10-15% margin.
why_now: NIH funding disruption and higher reagent prices from tariffs (verify current tariff levels) make labs care about every wasted dollar in 2025-26. Vision LLMs make label OCR and claim drafting almost free. Reproducibility pressure is high and the NIH is pushing rigor. Vendors are consolidating, and challenger brands need a credible independent signal to displace incumbents.
revenue_model: Subscription per lab or per core. A 10-15% margin on group-buy locked-lot sales. Success-fee or flat fee on recovered credits. Later, paid lot-analytics dashboards for challenger vendors and distributors.
non_obvious_insight: The certificate of analysis tests the vendor's assay, not yours. The only real lot-quality signal is 'the lab down the hall using my cell type', and that signal already circulates informally by hallway lore. Nobody has digitized it because no single lab has enough data. The warranty-claim refund is the Trojan horse: it gives the user immediate ROI, so people log lot numbers without being asked, and it produces the data moat.
first_30_days: Build a no-code MVP: a forwarding inbox plus a form that pulls lot number and catalog number and drafts claim emails. Recruit 15 labs from organoid and iPSC Slack and Discord channels and postdoc association lists. Offer 3 months free plus a 'we file it for you' concierge. File the first 30 claims by hand to learn each vendor's rules. Show each lab the dollars recovered. Convert to $99/month once the first credit lands. In parallel, pick one product (for example BME or FBS) and quote a pooled lot reservation to 10 pilot labs.

title: Solar Monitoring Data as Appliance Stethoscope
one_liner: Use the consumption data already sitting in installers' monitoring portals to spot dying air conditioners, resistance heat, hidden EVs and always-on pool pumps, then sell verified leads to HVAC and electrical contractors with a share back to the installer.
customer: HVAC and heat-pump contractors, EV-charger electricians and pool contractors pay per verified lead ($100-300). Installers earn a 20-30% revenue share. A later payer could be home-warranty companies and insurers who want early-failure signals.
problem: Post-2025, residential solar installers are short of revenue and sit on 500-5,000 past customers with monitoring already attached. HVAC contractors pay $150-500 per lead and spend most of their marketing budget in peak summer emergencies. Nobody mines the consumption stream (Enphase, SolarEdge and Tesla gateways record it every 5-15 minutes), where a failing compressor, a home heated by resistance strips or a new EV shows up clearly.
solution: Install-side product called Home Energy Plus. The installer emails past customers an opt-in for a free annual system checkup, connecting to their monitoring account through the OEM's API. An anomaly model flags: an AC drawing 25%+ more than on comparable weather days, short cycling, high winter baseline (resistance heat), overnight EV signature, pool pump running 24 hours. The customer gets a plain-language report ('your AC is likely low on refrigerant; a $99 tune-up now avoids a July failure'). Contractors bid for the lead in their service area, and the installer is paid a share. Homeowners can opt out at any time.
why_now: Federal 25C and 25D credits ended Dec 31, 2025, so heat-pump and HVAC contractors need intent-rich leads. Installers need recurring revenue from existing customers as new-install volume falls in 2026. OEM monitoring APIs are open to owner-authorized apps, and anomaly-detection models are cheap. Spring and fall shoulder seasons are when contractors most want planned replacements.
revenue_model: $100-300 per lead depending on trade and job size, split 70/30 with the installer. Optional $5-10 a month homeowner subscription for continuing reports. Later, sell early-failure signals to home-warranty companies at a per-home annual fee.
non_obvious_insight: An installer's monitoring portal is a stethoscope for the whole house, but installers use it only to answer why production is low. The consumption side is unlabeled and unused. Also, homeowners already trust the installer, and consent to share data is easiest to get from that relationship. A planned replacement in shoulder season is worth more to an HVAC company than an emergency job in July, because it fills idle crews.
first_30_days: Sign 3 installers with 1,000+ customers on Enphase or SolarEdge. Send the opt-in as a free annual checkup. Analyze 300 homes' historical data by hand and code up the first two signatures (AC and resistance heat). Produce 30 personalized reports. Sell the first 10 leads to two HVAC contractors at $150 each and measure close rate. Draft the consent and data-use terms with a privacy lawyer.

title: Grid-Paid Spiffs for Water Heater Installers
one_liner: Make the plumber on the emergency water-heater call the distribution channel for heat pump water heaters and grid demand-response programs, with a same-day rebate stack, an electrician handoff and a per-device bounty paid to the tech.
customer: Virtual power plant aggregators, utility demand-response and efficiency-program administrators and manufacturers' connected-water-heater programs, who pay for enrolled devices. The plumbing shop and tech are the paid channel partners.
problem: Roughly 9 million water heaters get replaced each year and the large majority are emergency replacements decided in a four-hour window, standing in an inch of water. The plumber decides what goes in. Utilities and aggregators spend hundreds of dollars per customer on mailers and rebates that almost nobody uses, because the customer does not think about the water heater until it dies. Plumbers install the 50-gallon tank on the truck because a heat pump unit needs a 240V circuit, a condensate drain, clearance and paperwork, plumbers do not do electrical, and a callback eats a week of margin. The federal 25C credit ended December 31, 2025, so what is left are state and utility rebates that customers cannot pre-approve while the old tank is leaking.
solution: An install-day tool for the tech's phone. Enter the ZIP, the current heater and a photo of the panel and get back every stackable rebate for that address with the homeowner's net cost against a like-for-like tank (a 20-second sales conversation). Route the 240V circuit to a pre-priced partner electrician for a next-day flat fee, or steer to a 120V plug-in heat pump model when the panel is tight. At install, scan the QR on the heater to enroll it in the aggregator or utility program with the customer's consent. Pay the tech a same-week spiff and the shop a fee. We handle rebate paperwork in the background so the plumber's job ends when the tank is set.
why_now: Federal tax credits are gone, so utility and state programs and point-of-sale rebates now decide the price difference. Virtual power plants and utility demand-response are actively looking for cheap, high-volume device enrollment. Manufacturers now ship connected and 120V plug-in heat pump units that remove the biggest install objections. The labor-constrained plumber has never been offered a spiff that is bigger than the hassle.
revenue_model: Take 20-30% of the per-device enrollment or midstream incentive paid by the aggregator or utility (typically $200-600 per device is now spent on customer acquisition), pay $50-100 to the tech and $50-100 to the shop, and keep the rest. Add a per-install electrician referral fee and a $99 per month shop subscription for the rebate engine once volumes justify it.
non_obvious_insight: The whole electrification industry markets to homeowners, who make no decision until the tank fails. The only person who actually decides is a plumber with a 20-minute window, paid by the ticket and hating callbacks. Plumbers will not sell a heat pump water heater because it is a worse day for them, not because they are anti-green. Fix the day and the channel opens, and the spiff is the cheapest customer acquisition the grid will ever buy.
first_30_days: Choose one territory with a live heat pump water heater rebate plus a demand-response or VPP program (e.g. Massachusetts, Colorado, the Pacific Northwest or California). Build the rebate stack for that utility in a spreadsheet and a text-message enrollment link. Sign 5 shops and 1 partner electrician. Pitch an aggregator or the program administrator a pilot of 100 enrolled devices at an agreed bounty, with the spiff paid manually at first.

title: Fandom Events in Empty Cinema Auditoriums
one_liner: A rights-plus-ticketing agency that fills weekday auditoriums with VTuber concert viewings, esports finals and game-reveal nights, splitting the box office with cinema chains.
customer: Fandom promoters and community organizers, VTuber agencies, esports and game publishers wanting fan events, and regional cinema chains as venue partners. Fans pay $15-30.
problem: Overseas viewers are about 30% of Hololive viewership and roughly 10B yen of revenue, yet have no communal way to attend, while Sphere-scale venues cost hundreds of millions and Live Nation controls arenas. Independent organizers rent bars with poor AV and no rights.
solution: Package a dark room, great sound and a projection booth with the rest of the event: sublicensed rights, a licensed live feed, all-in-price ticketing, cosplay contests and merch tables. Start with regional independent chains and a fixed menu of event formats.
why_now: Hololive concert revenue grew 18.7% and overseas fandom is underserved. The FTC's all-in-pricing rule and the Live Nation verdict make promoters and fans look for alternatives to arena ticketing. Cinemas still need non-Hollywood content for off-peak seats.
revenue_model: 15-25% of ticket revenue plus $2-8k per event for rights and technical fees, with cinemas taking a box-office split and concessions.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce ingredient in experience-economy fandom is not a $2B dome, it's a room with audio and projection, which cinemas already own and leave empty midweek. Everyone is chasing IP-in-space capex while the arbitrage is empty seats.
first_30_days: Pitch 5 independent cinema owners on a revenue split. Sign one rights-cleared event, such as a fighting-game grand finals viewing or a licensed VTuber concert screening. Run three test events by day 45 and measure fill rate and concession spend.

title: Front Door for AI Callers at Local Businesses
one_liner: A phone-number layer that recognizes when the caller is an AI agent, answers instantly with pre-authorized quotes and availability, and routes real customers to humans.
customer: Owner-operated local service businesses (salons, groomers, HVAC and plumbing, auto shops, cleaners) with 1-20 staff, reached via marketing agencies and booking or field-service platforms. AI receptionist vendors are later licensees.
problem: Google's 'Have AI check pricing' agentic calling has rolled out to US Search users and expanded to home services in summer 2026. Businesses now get AI callers that tie up staff and harvest prices, and owners cannot tell agents from customers. In Microsoft's Magentic Marketplace simulation, buyer agents heavily favored the first proposal they received, so fast structured answers win business.
solution: Answer with an agent detector and an agent lane. If the caller identifies as or behaves like an AI (or presents a signed handshake), reply with a spoken and machine-readable quote from the owner's rate card and calendar within owner-set bounds, and log the outcome. Real customers go to humans. Publish a URL or DTMF handshake so compliant agents can switch from speech to structured data, the Gibberlink idea done with production-grade channels. Analytics show which agents call and quote win rates.
why_now: Agentic calling is live at Google scale, AI receptionists are common, and the 2025 Gibberlink demo proved the handshake idea but remains a proof of concept. Production agent protocols (MCP, A2A) do not cover phone calls to small businesses.
revenue_model: $49-$149/month per location, agency white-label deals, and later per-verified-handshake fees from agent platforms.
non_obvious_insight: The phone is the API of the local economy and both ends are becoming machines that still talk in speech. Whoever owns the switch-to-data handshake and the seller's rate-card truth owns local agent commerce, and speed to first quote may matter more than price.
first_30_days: Build the call flow on a telephony API. Recruit 20 salons, groomers and HVAC shops through 3 local marketing agencies, log the AI calls they receive (many owners are unaware), and show AI calls answered and quotes won. Charge $79/month.

title: Phantom Load Vetting Desk for Rural Utilities
one_liner: A fee-based 'is this data center developer real?' diligence service for electric co-ops and municipal utilities drowning in 100-1,000 MW inquiries from shell LLCs.
customer: G&T and distribution electric cooperatives, municipal utilities and PUDs (5-person engineering staffs, no data center experience). Secondary: state economic development offices and county governments granting abatements. The utility or its G&T pays per inquiry or on retainer.
problem: Every small utility with transmission access is now getting inquiries for 200-1,000 MW campuses from LLCs formed 90 days ago. Each one eats study money, planning time and political capital, and a wrong bet strands ratepayer-funded infrastructure. Texas's proposed SB 6 rule (16 TAC 25.194, final rule due by end of 2026) would require $50,000/MW of financial security before a study and disclosure of duplicate requests. That pushes speculators into neighboring states and co-ops with softer tariffs. Small utilities have no way to tell a real project from a PowerPoint.
solution: A standardized 12-point 'physical reality' test built from paper trails that real projects leave and phantom ones cannot. (1) Air permit applications for generators, where the genset count implies the MW. (2) An OEM order acknowledgment or slot reservation for MV transformers and switchgear, plus a delivery date that fits the claimed energization date. (3) Recorded site control (deed or option). (4) Water and stormwater filings. (5) A named tenant LOI or offtaker. (6) A GC or EPC that has actually built a campus. (7) A financing letter. (8) Tax-abatement filings. (9) LLC principals cross-checked against other states' filings, to catch the same MW shopped to five utilities. (10) A power-density and cooling design consistent with the load ask. (11) Local land-use posture. (12) Team track record. The deliverable is a red/amber/green memo, a recommended security amount, and a milestone-gated study structure the utility can put in its ESA. Add-ons are a large-load tariff and ESA term-sheet template and a duplicate-request registry that co-ops in a region can pool.
why_now: Large-load tariffs and collateral rules are landing right now: Texas SB 6 (signed June 2025, PUCT rule proposed March 2026, final expected by 12/31/2026), plus AEP Ohio-style minimum-demand tariffs. Each new collateral regime displaces phantom load to the next-weakest utility. Transformer lead times of 3-5 years and switchgear sold out into 2028 mean that a real project without an equipment slot is not real, which gives a very cheap and reliable test. About half of announced 2026 builds are delayed or canceled, so utilities are burned and skeptical.
revenue_model: $7.5K-25K per inquiry vetting memo; $60K-150K/yr retainers for G&T co-ops that field 10+ inquiries a year; $25K-50K one-time tariff/ESA template packages; later a subscription to a multi-utility duplicate-request registry. Utilities can often pass the cost to the applicant as a study-deposit line item.
non_obvious_insight: Outsiders think the hard part of large-load planning is forecasting demand. Insiders know real projects are betrayed by equipment, not slides. A serious 300 MW developer has a transformer slot, a generator count on an air permit and a GC on payroll before the utility ever hears the name. A phantom has none of those. The tell is the logistics trail, and nobody at a 5-person co-op knows where to look. Texas's high collateral will also export the phantom problem to everyone else.
first_30_days: Build scrapers for state air-permit databases in 6-8 states and county deed/LLC records for 3 co-op service territories. Ask 3 co-op contacts (via state electric cooperative associations or a G&T's planning group) for their last 10 inquiries and run free back-tests on how they turned out. Publish a one-page '12 signs your data center inquiry is real' on LinkedIn and co-op association channels. Convert the first 2-3 into paid $7.5K memos on live inquiries and ask for a G&T retainer.
